title: Girl Who Chased Jets Is Now IAF's First Woman Fighter Combat Leader
excerpt: Squadron Leader Bhawana Kanth graduated from the 20-week Fighter Combat Leader course at TACDE Gwalior — the IAF's equivalent of Top Gun — a decade after becoming one of India's first women fighter pilots.
body:
• Squadron Leader Bhawana Kanth has become the first woman officer in the Indian Air Force to complete the Fighter Combat Leader (FCL) course, finishing the 20-week programme at the Tactics and Air Combat Development Establishment (TACDE) in Gwalior on August 6, 2026.
  • The FCL course — often likened to the US Navy's Top Gun school — is the IAF's most selective tactical qualification; roughly 1% of fighter pilots are chosen for each intake, and a significant share do not graduate.
  • Kanth, who flies the Su-30MKI, was commissioned in June 2016 as one of the first three women in the IAF's fighter stream. She was the first Indian woman cleared for daytime combat missions (2019) and received the Nari Shakti Puraskar in 2020.
  • As a Fighter Combat Leader she returns to her squadron tasked with shaping air combat tactics, planning weapons deployment and training the frontline pilots who fly after her.

Squadron Leader Bhawana Kanth has carved another first into Indian military aviation. The Su-30MKI pilot has become the first woman officer in the Indian Air Force to complete the Fighter Combat Leader (FCL) course, the service's most demanding tactical qualification, graduating from the 20-week programme at the Tactics and Air Combat Development Establishment (TACDE) in Gwalior on August 6, 2026.

The achievement caps a decade-long climb that began when Kanth was one of three women commissioned into the IAF's fighter stream in June 2016 — an experiment the force had approved only months earlier. Ten years on, she stands at the top of the IAF's tactical hierarchy, qualifying in a course often compared to the US Navy's Top Gun school.

"I had no idea that women don't get fighters."

— Squadron Leader Bhawana Kanth, speaking to The Times of India

Context & Background

Kanth was born on December 1, 1992, in Barauni, Begusarai, Bihar, and grew up in the state before studying medical electronics at BMS College of Engineering in Bengaluru. She joined the IAF after the fighter stream was opened to women in 2015, and was commissioned in June 2016 alongside Avani Chaturvedi and Mohana Singh — the first women ever to enter the fighter cockpit.

Her career has been a sequence of firsts. She flew the MiG-21 Bison — one of the IAF's oldest and most unforgiving jets — from an airbase in Bikaner, Rajasthan, flying her first solo sortie in March 2018. In May 2019 she became the first Indian woman fighter pilot cleared for daytime combat missions. She featured on the IAF's Republic Day tableau in 2021, received the Nari Shakti Puraskar — India's highest civilian honour for women — in 2020, and later transitioned to the twin-engine Su-30MKI, one of the IAF's primary multirole fighters. She has led elements of the Republic Day flypast and is currently posted in Punjab.

The IAF announced her FCL graduation on its official channels, releasing photographs of her being felicitated by a senior officer at TACDE. The course itself covers advanced air-to-air and air-to-ground tactics, mission planning, electronic warfare, weapons employment and leadership in high-intensity scenarios. Only about 1% of the force's fighter pilots are selected for each intake, and graduates return to their units as the authorities on operational doctrine and combat manoeuvring. Her milestone drew praise from Union Minister Smriti Irani, who highlighted Kanth's progression from pioneering fighter pilot to elite combat leader.

Impact & Analysis

The significance of the FCL qualification is professional, not symbolic. Fighter combat leaders decide how squadrons train, plan missions and fight — their influence outlasts their own operational postings by years. Kanth now holds a direct hand in shaping the tactics of the pilots, including the women, who will fly after her. Defence observers note the achievement underscores how far the operational roles open to women have expanded in the decade since the fighter stream opened on an experimental basis.

It also lands at a moment when the IAF is preparing for modern warfare challenges — unmanned systems, network-centric operations — that demand exactly the kind of tactical planning the FCL course teaches. Kanth's graduation puts a woman officer at the centre of that doctrinal work.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Kanth's story has become a touchstone of Nari Shakti — the idea of women's power — in its most literal form. Her trajectory, from a small town in Bihar to the IAF's premier air combat school, is followed closely by Indian communities abroad who track the military's modernisation with particular pride. It also resonates beyond India: she joins a very small number of women worldwide qualified to lead frontline fighter combat operations, at a time when diaspora conversations about women in uniform — from the Indian armed forces to Western militaries — are more active than ever.

What's Next

Kanth returns to her Su-30MKI squadron as a fighter combat leader, tasked with refining frontline tactics and training the next intake of pilots. The wider arc continues: the cohort that began with three women in 2016 has widened considerably, with officers such as Shivangi Singh going on to fly the Rafale. The next milestone to watch is whether the FCL course — and the senior operational command roles it feeds — becomes a regular, rather than exceptional, destination for women in the IAF's fighter stream.
